title: Kurma
hook: the nectar's out, Mohini pours, and one sip can't be taken back
tomorrow: the earth itself sinks into the sea. who goes down for it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kurma, and the treasures: holy events or the inner churning, with both readings agreeing on the order. The nectar's finally out, and everyone grabs. Who gets a taste?

The first spoonful of something sweet after a long, hard day: people slow down for it. The pot of amrita is out of the sea, carried by Dhanvantari, and the moment it appears, the asuras grab it. They pulled half the rope; they want it all. The gods can't win it back by force. Then a woman walks into the middle of the quarrel, so lovely that everyone stops arguing.
screen: `THE FIRST SWEET SPOONFUL.` → `THE ASURAS GRAB THE POT.` → `A WOMAN WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: She's Mohini, Vishnu in a new form. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, the asuras hand her the pot themselves and ask her to share it out. She seats the two sides in rows and pours for the gods. One asura, Rahu, sees what's happening. He slips into the gods' row in disguise and gets a sip. The Sun and the Moon spot him and call out, and Vishnu's discus cuts off his head. But the nectar has already touched his mouth, so the head lives on. Some tellings say that's why, now and then, Rahu swallows the Sun or the Moon and they slip out again: an eclipse. So this is a story that comes down to the senses. The whole churning, the poison, the treasures, the tortoise holding for all of it, ends in a taste. And a taste, the story says, can't be taken back. Rahu got one sip, and it stayed. One more thing the text doesn't hide: the asuras did half the work and got none of the nectar. In the Bhagavata's telling, the effort on both sides was the same and the results weren't, and the text puts the difference down to who took refuge in Vishnu.
screen: `MOHINI POURS THE NECTAR.` · `RAHU SLIPS INTO THE ROW.` · `ONE SIP CAN'T BE TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `SAME EFFORT, DIFFERENT FRUIT.`

segments.voice: If you have water or anything small to eat, take one sip or one bite and don't swallow right away. Let it sit on your tongue: the temperature, the taste, what changes as you wait. Then swallow, and notice what stays. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for it.
Kurma: the tortoise who held the mountain so the nectar could come up at last.
Hold onto this one: Kurma, who held the whole churning, all the way to the taste. Rest well.

howItsDone: The story of Mohini and the amrita is retold from the Bhagavata Purana, and in some places Rahu is named in traditional explanations of eclipses.

fork.setup: Rahu sits in the gods' row in disguise and gets one sip before he's caught. in the story, what happens to that sip?
options: it stays; his head lives on, because the nectar touched his mouth.
it's taken back the moment he's caught.
it turns to poison because he cheated.
fork.reveal: the discus cuts off his head, but the nectar has already touched his mouth, so the head lives. a taste, in this story, can't be taken back.

original.note: Sanskrit amrita: the nectar the whole churning was for.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gods simply win the nectar by being stronger.
what it means: Vishnu, as Mohini, pours it for the gods, and Rahu's stolen sip can't be undone.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata 8.8–8.9, Mohini and Rahu; the text says the effort was equal and puts the difference down to refuge in Vishnu.
recall: rises from the sea and chooses Vishnu

chat.says: nani made kheer and called it 'amrita.' dad laughed for the first time since the fight. what's she saying?
options: after the poison and the pulling, this is the sweet part it was for.
it's just her word for dessert; amrita means rice pudding.
she's saying the fight never really happened at all.
chat.meaning: In the churning, poison came first and the amrita came last: the sweet thing the whole hard work was for.

Mohini.meaning: Vishnu's lovely form who shares out the nectar

Rahu.meaning: the asura who sneaks a sip of nectar

Dhanvantari.meaning: physician of the gods, who carries the amrita

asuras.meaning: the gods' rivals, who grab the pot

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.8–8.9 (the asuras seize the amrita; Mohini; Rahu in the gods' row; the Sun and Moon; the discus; equal effort, different results)
